```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(sf)
library(readr)
library(leaflet)
library(scales)

terminals <- read_csv("data/processed/lng_terminals.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
```

## What this is

I study international affairs, and I wrote the code for this as well. This started as a student project. When Russian pipeline gas stopped, the Baltic region built new coastal terminals to bring gas in by ship, and I wanted to map them and work out how exposed each one looks from public data alone.

In 2021 the eight countries on that sea took about 70 bcm (billion cubic metres) of gas from Russia by pipe. By 2023 the same Eurostat series was down to almost nothing. Five working coastal LNG terminals (LNG is liquefied natural gas, which arrives by ship), plus a sixth planned at Gdańsk, can land about 23 bcm a year between them. That is roughly a third of what stopped arriving. The rest of the gap closed because demand fell and because gas still comes in by pipe from Norway and the west.

On a normal year, then, the region is not short of gas. What interested me was how concentrated those terminals are, how close they sit to Russian territory, and how much of the supply run depends on ships coming through the Danish Straits. I score each terminal on those three things. The weights are my own choice, and you can change them on the Analysis page.

Nord Stream was blown up in 2022, Balticconnector was damaged in 2023, and Estlink 2 was cut in 2024. Those events keep landing on the same stretch of geography, and that geography is what I map. The events themselves are left out of the score.

The terminal capacities are operator figures from 2024 and 2025, and import dependency comes from Eurostat for 2023. Every source I used is listed on the [Data](01-data.qmd) page.

So how concentrated is that infrastructure, and how exposed is it? On the map, each point is sized by capacity. Hover over one for its name, or click it for the figures.

```{r overview-map}
#| echo: false
source("scripts/basemap.R")
tb <- st_bbox(terminals)
leaflet(terminals) |>
  add_basemap() |>
  fitBounds(tb[["xmin"]] - 1.5, tb[["ymin"]] - 0.8,
            tb[["xmax"]] + 1.5, tb[["ymax"]] + 0.8) |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    radius      = ~rescale(capacity_bcm, to = c(5, 15)),
    color       = map_ink, weight = 1,
    fillColor   = map_mark, fillOpacity = 0.85,
    label       = ~name,
    popup       = ~paste0("<b>", name, "</b><br>", country,
                          "<br>", capacity_bcm, " bcm/yr<br>", status))
```

## What I found

The numbers are on the [Analysis](02-analysis.qmd) page. Capacities move, and I would read them as a picture of the pattern rather than as a precise measurement.

Świnoujście in Poland and Mukran in Germany hold about three fifths of the operating import capacity. The northeast gets by on one or two terminals each, with Inkoo serving the Gulf of Finland and Klaipėda serving Lithuania. In all, five working sites replaced a continental pipe network, and Gdańsk is still only planned.

The terminals closest to Russian territory are the small ones. Hamina sits at the eastern end of the Gulf of Finland, while Klaipėda and Gdańsk are next door to Kaliningrad. The two largest terminals are among the farthest from Russia. Because of that mismatch, I did not rank on size alone.

Every cargo still comes in through the Danish Straits. The Kiel Canal is the other door, and it is too small for LNG carriers. Once a ship is inside the sea, the terminals up in the Gulf of Finland are the longest run.

Finland and Lithuania built well beyond their own demand, while Germany and Poland, which burn much more gas, cover only part of theirs by sea. In effect the northeast built a buffer that its neighbours draw on. If I had to take a single finding into a conversation, it would be this one. The terminals sitting closest to Russia are also the ones carrying spare capacity for the rest of the region.

## How the score is built

Each terminal gets a score built from three ingredients:

- how close it is to Russian territory (I gave this 0.4, the largest share),
- how much of the region's import capacity it holds (0.3),
- how long its supply route past the Danish Straits runs (0.3).

I gave proximity the most weight because the question is about exposure to one neighbour, and distance is the most direct thing the public data will support. Capacity matters since a larger terminal does more damage if it stops. The Straits are in there for the route, as a cargo bound for the Gulf of Finland has a longer run once it is inside the sea.

Those weights are a judgement call, and other people might reasonably pick different ones. If you want to test them, drag them on the Analysis page and see how much the order moves.

## Disruptions since 2022

Since 2022, energy and data links under the Baltic have been damaged several times, mostly by ships dragging their anchors across the seabed.

| Date | Asset | What happened |
|------|-------|---------------|
| Sep 2022 | Nord Stream 1 and 2 | Subsea gas pipelines ruptured by underwater explosions off Bornholm. |
| Oct 2023 | Balticconnector | The Finland-Estonia gas pipeline and a telecoms cable were damaged by a ship's anchor. The pipeline was shut for six months and returned to commercial use on 22 April 2024. |
| Dec 2024 | Estlink 2 | The Estonia-Finland power cable and four telecoms cables were cut on Christmas Day; a shadow-fleet tanker is the prime suspect. Repairs ran into 2025 and the link returned to commercial use on 20 June 2025. |

I have kept those events as background, outside the score. The [Analysis](02-analysis.qmd) page maps the corridors and shows which ones have been hit.

Sources: [Balticconnector return to service (Gasgrid)](https://gasgrid.fi/en/2024/04/19/balticconnector-in-commercial-use-from-monday-22-april-onwards/),
[Estlink 2 return to service (Fingrid)](https://www.fingrid.fi/en/news/news/2025/estlink-2-electricity-transmission-link-returns-to-commercial-use/),
[Estlink 2 incident (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Estlink_2_incident).

## What I would take from this

The EU has a test called N-1, which asks whether a country can still meet demand if its single largest piece of supply infrastructure fails. If I borrow that idea and knock out each country's largest terminal, Finland is left with Hamina, covering about a fifth of demand, and Lithuania, Poland and Germany are left with no seaborne capacity at all. To be fair to them, they are not failing the real N-1 test, which also counts pipes and storage. The trouble is that their fallback is the same set of links that have already been damaged.

Estonia, Latvia and Sweden have no terminal of their own, and their gas comes through neighbours over pipes and cables such as the Balticconnector. That layer has already been hit.

All eight countries share one entrance through the Danish Straits. Anything that watches that stretch of water (the kind of patrol NATO stood up after the December 2024 cable cuts) covers the whole region at once.

FSRUs (moored ships that act as floating terminals) were quick to bring in and can be moved, but there are only a few of them and they are on charter. Mukran lost about half its capacity when a second ship came off charter. That is why I count it at about 6 bcm rather than the 13.5 bcm still quoted in a lot of headlines.

## Limitations

What this measures is geographic exposure. It says nothing about the probability that anything will happen. A terminal close to a maritime boundary is just a fact about a map.

- The score uses distance and capacity share as stand-ins (proxies) for exposure. If you change the weights, the ranking moves.
- It is one snapshot in time, and capacities, routes and terminals all change.
- I compiled the capacities from operator reporting and Global Energy Monitor, and they are current to 2024 and 2025. The dependence figures are Eurostat for 2023. The [Data](01-data.qmd) page has the detail.
- The 2023 to 2025 cable and pipeline incidents are background only. They are not events in the score.

I would treat this as a way of seeing where the exposure sits. It is not a forecast.

## Terms

- **LNG (liquefied natural gas):** natural gas chilled to a liquid so it can be
  carried by ship rather than a pipeline.
- **LNG terminal:** the coastal site where those ships unload and the cargo is
  turned back into gas for the pipeline network. Some are built on land; some are
  a moored ship, known as an FSRU (a floating storage and regasification unit).
- **Capacity (bcm):** how much gas a terminal can bring in over a year, measured
  in billion cubic metres.
- **Import dependency:** the share of a country's gas that comes from abroad
  rather than from its own production.
